title: Pipkin and the Porthaven Trophy
markdown:
Porthaven’s wind was not merely weather. It was a boisterous fellow with a taste for drama, whipping the sea into white streaks and making the cobbles shine like wet slate. Pipkin the postmistress preferred tides. A letter for Mrs. Higgins, tucked into her rosebush. A sturdy parcel for the lighthouse keeper, delivered with a polite nod. Every item catalogued, sorted, dispatched. Her whiskers twitched not with excitement but with a quiet dread of anything unscheduled. The thought of a stage, of the whole town looking, made her paws feel like cold damp pebbles.

This year there was the Porthaven Lighthouse Trophy, awarded for the most efficient postal service. Pipkin wanted it. Not for fanfare. For the validation of careful work: a handshake, a quiet thank you, and the desk remaining a desk. Failure would leave a whisper of inadequacy in the sorting room. The North Sea forecast was fierce. Mail had to get through.

Monday she still sorted by the window, tying string with the same knot her mother had taught her, labelling the lighthouse bag twice because once was never a kindness. By Wednesday the glass had begun to rattle. She left the well-worn stack of mailbags and the comfort of her labelled pigeonholes. A gale was coming, a real humdinger, and Friday’s Porthaven Regatta parade would close the main road. Her task, the one that made her whiskers vibrate: deliver a crucial telegram to Captain Cadfan at the docks before the road shut. If she missed him, he missed a business chance that could tug at half the town. The clock was the incoming tide, already beginning to surge, licking the lowest steps as if tasting the day.

The wind howled. It rattled the post office’s bones. Pipkin’s fur stood. Could she cross slick moss-covered cobbles that now felt like greased ice?

A shadow. A massive white shape erupted from behind a stack of fishing nets. Bartholomew the goose, flapping with unwarranted gusto, honked like a foghorn with opinions. He blasted a passing seagull. The gull, in a panicked dive, dropped a partially eaten fish squarely onto the telegram.

Pipkin’s heart hammered. The whole town might as well have been watching. She froze. Bartholomew, oblivious, continued his noisy pronouncements, as if the docks were a concert hall and he the only booked act.

She nearly turned back.

Then Mina, her badger friend, appeared, sturdy as bedrock under shifting sand. “Pipkin. The telegram. Don’t let him spoil it.” Firm. Kind.

A tiny spark. Pipkin ducked under Bartholomew’s flailing wings; feathers brushed her nose. Her paws slipped on kelp. The telegram, now damp and slightly fishy, fluttered. She lunged, ungraceful, and snatched it as a rogue wave crashed over the pier, soaking her tail and the document’s edges. Close. Very close.

The gale worsened. The sky went bruised purple. Nets snapped like wet flags. Pipkin kept to the lee of the crates, telegram pressed to her chest, fish-scent and salt fighting for the paper. Mina paced her for a stretch, then peeled off toward the warehouse with a look that said the rest was Pipkin’s. At the far end of the docks Captain Cadfan’s face was etched with worry. He took the telegram, unfolded it with trembling paws, and when he looked up his gruff nod was a whole weather system of relief. “You came through,” he said, which was as close as the Captain came to poetry.

Victory, of a sort, was in reach. Then came the awards, in the town square under newly lit lanterns. Chatter. Anticipation. Bartholomew, now wearing a festive if crooked red ribbon, honked a triumphant off-key fanfare. Mayor Gable, portly, booming, cleared his throat.

“And the Porthaven Lighthouse Trophy, for outstanding postal service, goes to Pipkin, our dedicated postmistress.”

Applause. Whistles. Cheers. Pipkin’s fur felt thin, as if the noise could pass through her. Every eye. She wanted the salty mist.

The trophy was cool and heavy. The crowd filled her head. Spray that usually comforted now felt like icy fingers. Bartholomew preened by the table, honking, a mirror of all that attention. Pipkin wanted to flee. She looked at the trophy, then at her favourite smooth stone, the one she kept in her pocket for quiet moments. She could leave it on the table’s edge, a small offering to the life she craved. The stone slipped. It landed with a soft thud, unnoticed. A small cost. It felt like giving away a piece of solitude.

“Pipkin?” Mina nudged her snout, warm breath. “It’s just people. They’re happy for you. Because you’re good at what you do. That’s all.”

Pipkin looked at the trophy. Polished metal caught the lanterns. Not a brand. Recognition. Quiet excellence, made visible. Then a familiar honk. Bartholomew had spotted a dropped crumpet and waddled toward it with determined purpose, eyes on the prize. He was not seeking an audience. He was doing his goose thing.

She stayed.

The next morning the trophy sat on her desk, less a burden than a well-earned paperweight. A delivery waited at the furthest cottage, along a path Bartholomew often inconveniently used. At the familiar bend he was mid-squawk, body blocking the way, pecking at something unseen.

Pipkin did not freeze. She took a breath of salt air. “Bartholomew,” she said, voice steadier than she expected, “a small detour might be required for this delivery.”

He blinked his beady eyes, gave a soft honk, and shuffled aside, his noise dropping to a murmur, as if the request had been a kind of stamp. She delivered the letter. The rosebush route, later, felt the same as always, except that her paws no longer waited for the town to look. The stone was gone. The trophy caught a thin strip of morning on the desk, and Pipkin catalogued the next bag as if the wind, for once, could wait its turn.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
